newsitem.title: USA: Newfoundland aims to revive big hydro project.
newsitem.headline: Newfoundland aims to revive big hydro project.

text.p: Deregulation of energy markets in the United States could spell the revival of long-contemplated plans for a huge hydroelectric project in Newfoundland, Premier Brian Tobin said on Wednesday.

Tobin, leader of Canada's most economically depressed province, said the proposed Lower Churchill River project could export some of its estimated 17 billion kilowatt hours of power to New England states, making it more viable.
The plan, which won environmental approval in the early 1980s, is one of the most economically and environmentally sound on the continent, Tobin said.
"There is a clear, competitive alternative," he said at the Annual Conference for the New England Governors and Eastern Canadian Premiers, held in Newport
"We don't believe raising financing is a problem," he said. Later, he added: "I think this is a project that is going to happen."
Tobin said he was seeking public and private partners, possibly including some in the United States, to get the plan off the ground.
He declined to speculate about whether his province would become a competitor of neighboring Quebec in producing energy and exporting it to power-hungry New England.
How closely the two Canadian provinces cooperate could hinge on the handling of a long-running dispute over an electricity contract from the existing Churchill Falls facility.

Newfoundland is locked into supplying Hydro-Quebec with low-cost electricity from upper Churchill Falls as part of a long-term deal signed before world energy prices jumped in the 1970s. The province has tried to renegotiate higher rates from Quebec, so far to no avail.
Hydro-Quebec has said it spends about C$100 million a year for Churchill Falls power and takes in about C$750 million reselling it to Quebec and New England customers.
Asked whether he had discussed energy at the conference with Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard, Tobin told reporters: "We've had energetic discussions."

Bouchard said current talks between the two provinces about managing energy development were expected to be wrapped up in September, but he declined to say specifically whether the long-term supply contracts would be re-examined.

Both Newfoundland and Quebec are free to develop their own power capacity, he said. "If there were other possibilities elsewhere, if some people are willing to talk with us about what happened in the past, what is the present situation, and what should happen in the future...then we are quite ready to sit down and discuss with an open mind."
Bouchard called government-owned Hydro-Quebec a natural partner for Newfoundland in any hydroelectric developments.
If the lower Churchill project was to proceed, Tobin estimated it could begin produce power by around 2006. "It's a realistic time-frame," he said.
Both Maine and Massachusetts officials expressed interest in the potential new supply of power.
